title: Moody's: US Life Insurers' Private and Illiquid Bonds Reach $807 Billion, 20% of Fixed Income, With Concentration and PIK Risks to Watch
summary: Moody's report of June 8, 2026 says private and illiquid bonds at US life insurers reached $807 billion at end-2025, up from $685 billion, with the ten largest holding 44% and four areas flagged for monitoring.
description:
Private credit has become a core part of how US life insurers invest, and Moody's Ratings says that the shift carries risks that deserve close attention. In a report published on June 8, 2026, and covered by Insurance Business and Reinsurance News, Moody's said the industry's private and illiquid bonds reached $807 billion at year-end 2025. That is about 20% of the industry's $4 trillion fixed income portfolio, up from $685 billion, or 18%, a year earlier, an increase of $122 billion in one year. Moody's called the shift structural rather than cyclical. This article summarises the report as covered by those outlets. An earlier version relied mainly on the Barclays growth figure and the Proskauer default index; the Moody's figures themselves are now set out first.

How does Moody's define the assets? According to Reinsurance News, Moody's defines private credit as non-bank lending. For insurers this includes commercial real estate and mortgage loans and traditional private placements. Of the $807 billion, bonds carrying a private-letter rating (PL) account for $483 billion, or 12% of bonds, Z-rated bonds for $81 billion, or about 2%, and other Level 3 holdings for $242 billion, or 6%. By composition, 64% is issuer credit obligations such as corporate debt, loans, project finance and REIT and BDC obligations, while 36% is asset-backed securities. Moody's says growth is spreading into real estate debt, infrastructure debt and asset-based finance, including private ABS, fund finance and data centre securitisations. Demand is driven by higher risk-adjusted yields and by more privately originated credit opportunities. Insurers get access through direct origination platforms, partnerships with asset managers and affiliated asset management structures.

What are the four areas Moody's is watching? First, concentration. The ten largest insurers hold $352 billion, or 44%, of the private illiquid bonds, while holding only 24% of total industry fixed income. Second, a widening credit-quality gap. Reinsurance News reports that 91% of the $807 billion carries an investment-grade-equivalent designation from the NAIC's Securities Valuation Office. By NAIC category, 49% is NAIC 1, 43% is NAIC 2 and 9% is below investment grade. The wider $4 trillion portfolio is 95% investment grade, with 59% in NAIC 1, 36% in NAIC 2 and 5% below investment grade. Moody's said that impairment rates in private credit could exceed those of liquid holdings in a downside scenario. Third, structural complexity. Asset-backed securities made up 38% of 2025 purchases, against 27% of existing holdings, which Moody's described as a deliberate strategic shift rather than passive drift. Fourth, payment-in-kind (PIK) instruments, where a borrower pays interest by adding to the debt instead of paying cash. PIK exposure equals 1.1% of statutory surplus, which Moody's views as moderate and not currently a material threat to balance sheets, but a possible late-cycle warning indicator. Insurers with the highest PIK balances relative to surplus include Resolution Life US, Genworth, Security Benefit, Wilton Re and Sammons, according to Reinsurance News. Moody's also cautions that headline PIK numbers may understate exposure, because bonds issued by business development companies may not show PIK even when their underlying borrowers use it.

Where is the stress emerging? Moody's says risks are emerging mainly in middle-market direct lending, where credit quality is weakening and borrower stress is rising. It also notes that, under narrower definitions of private credit, exposure is more limited, and that most reported exposure is investment grade. Moody's expects private credit corporate lending assets to exceed $2 trillion in 2026 and approach $4 trillion by 2030.

What other data points are cited? Insurance Business cites Barclays as finding that US life insurers' private credit holdings grew by more than 20% in 2025, with exposure above 15% of investments at some private-equity-affiliated insurers, including Apollo-backed Athene and KKR-backed Global Atlantic. It also cites the Proskauer Private Credit Default Index, which tracks 697 loans totalling $189.2 billion and reported a default rate of 2.73% in the first quarter of 2026, up from 1.84% two quarters earlier. Those figures come from different sources and use different definitions, so they should not be added together or compared directly with Moody's numbers.

What are regulators doing? The article says the National Association of Insurance Commissioners' 2025 Principles-Based Bond Definition lets it challenge the classification of complex assets, and that higher defaults could lead to capital charges. NAIC president Scott White has named transparency in life insurance portfolios as a top 2026 regulatory priority. The US Treasury convened domestic and international insurance regulators earlier in 2026 to discuss private credit risks. From year-end 2025 statutory filings, insurers must give more detailed bond disclosures, separating issuer credit obligations from structured ABS. In its commentary, Moody's stressed governance, stress testing and capital planning.

What does this mean for policyholders? Life insurers and annuity providers use long-term assets to match long-term promises, and illiquid assets can be a natural fit for that. The risk Moody's points to is not that policies are about to fail, but that concentration, weaker credit quality in some segments and complexity could make the system more vulnerable in a downturn. Those with annuities or life policies can look at their insurer's financial strength rating and ask how much of its portfolio is in private and structured assets.

The wider message is that private credit is no longer a niche for insurers. It is a material part of the industry's balance sheet, and its performance in a slowdown will be watched by ratings agencies, regulators and investors. This article summarises published reporting and is not investment advice.

key_points: Moody's says US life insurers' private and illiquid bonds reached $807 billion at year-end 2025, about 20% of a $4 trillion fixed income portfolio, up from $685 billion (18%) a year earlier.
The ten largest insurers hold $352 billion, or 44%, of those assets, although they hold only 24% of industry fixed income.
The private book is 43% NAIC 2 and 9% below investment grade, against 36% and 5% for the whole portfolio; 38% of 2025 purchases were asset-backed securities.
Payment-in-kind exposure is 1.1% of statutory surplus, which Moody's views as moderate but a possible late-cycle indicator.
Barclays found private credit holdings grew by more than 20% in 2025; Proskauer's default index rose to 2.73% in Q1 2026 from 1.84% two quarters earlier.
why_it_matters: Life insurers hold the long-term savings of millions of policyholders. If the private assets backing annuities and policies turn out harder to sell or weaker in credit quality than expected, the effect would reach customers, regulators and the wider credit market.

title: Singapore's New Integrated Shield Plan Rider Rules: A 5% Co-Payment Capped at S$6,000 and Premiums About 30% Lower
summary: From April 1, 2026, new Integrated Shield Plan riders in Singapore must include a 5% co-payment capped at S$6,000 a year and exclude the minimum deductible, a design the Ministry of Health says is about 30% cheaper than maximum-coverage riders.
description:
Singapore has changed the design of the optional riders that sit on top of Integrated Shield Plans, the private health insurance most residents use to upgrade the national MediShield Life scheme. The Ministry of Health (MOH) set out the framework in a parliamentary answer published on its website, with the new design taking effect on April 1, 2026. This article summarises what MOH says. An earlier version of this article also reported a medical inflation figure of 16.9%, an 84% premium cut by one insurer and a new MediSave rule for fertility preservation. MOH's own page on fertility preservation describes only the existing rule, which allows MediSave withdrawals up to a lifetime limit of S$15,000 per patient for treatments including egg freezing for medical reasons, and it does not confirm a June 2026 expansion, so those statements have been removed.

Some background helps. MediShield Life is the basic national health insurance scheme. Integrated Shield Plans (IPs) are private plans that add cover for private hospitals or higher ward classes. A rider is an optional add-on to an IP that pays some or all of the costs the IP leaves to the patient, namely the deductible, which is a fixed amount paid first, and the co-insurance, a percentage of the remaining bill. A rider that covers everything leaves the patient with almost nothing to pay, which makes the cost of treatment less visible and, as the minister put it, encourages over-servicing and over-consumption.

The new rules do three main things. First, the new riders include a co-payment of 5% of the bill, capped at S$6,000 a year, in addition to the deductible. Second, the new riders will not cover the minimum IP deductible, a fixed sum that the patient pays. Third, the rules apply to riders bought on or after November 27, 2025. Existing riders are not covered by the new requirements, and insurers decide how to handle them. The riders continue to protect against very large and unexpected bills, since the cap on the co-payment limits what a patient pays in a bad year.

MOH explains the change using cost data. The minister said premiums for IP riders for private hospitals grew by an average of 17% a year over the past three years, about double the growth of IP premiums themselves and faster than MediShield Life premiums. About 100,000 policyholders cancel or downgrade their riders each year, which suggests that cost is becoming a burden. The ministry said new riders are on average about 30% cheaper than existing maximum-coverage riders. As an example, a 60-year-old on maximum coverage could save about S$1,600 a year in premiums, or S$4,800 over three years, which the minister said would offset the higher co-payment for a typical procedure such as a S$3,300 knee replacement in a private hospital. These figures apply only to private hospital patients.

What will patients actually pay? MediSave, the national medical savings account, can be used to pay much of the co-payment. The minister projected that six in ten claimants would pay no cash out of pocket after using MediSave. Of the remaining four in ten, most with cash out-of-pocket would pay S$1,000 or less, and nearly all would pay S$3,000 or less. For a patient with a very large bill, the 5% co-payment is limited by the S$6,000 annual cap, and this is where the rider continues to provide protection.

The ministry also gave a second reason that is about the health system and not only cost. The share of patients treated in private hospitals fell from 15% in 2010 to 12% in 2020 and is now about 10%. The minister noted that some patients prefer public hospitals because of their range of specialties and holistic care. MOH will monitor the impact, especially in the short term, since some patients may switch to public hospitals to avoid the co-payment. It said it is expanding hospital beds and outpatient capacity and may introduce surge capacity for selected treatments. The page does not give targets or timelines for that capacity.

There are open questions that the parliamentary answer does not settle. It does not say whether insurers will allow policyholders to keep older, higher-coverage riders, or how older policyholders will be protected from reductions in cover. Those issues were raised in Parliament, but the answers recorded on the page do not address them directly. Readers who already hold a rider should check with their insurer or adviser what will happen to their policy at renewal, and whether switching would mean accepting the new co-payment.

Regulation is shared. MOH and the Monetary Authority of Singapore both oversee IP insurers. MOH sets key parameters such as co-payment and deductible rules and says it intervenes only when serious market failure appears. It consults insurers, providers and consumer representatives through the Multilateral Healthcare Insurance Committee.

For consumers, the practical message is to compare the lower premium with the higher out-of-pocket exposure, keeping in mind how much MediSave they have available to pay co-payments. For insurers, the reform is intended to slow claims growth and keep riders sustainable. For other markets facing rising health premiums, Singapore's approach, which keeps broad protection but restores some cost sharing, is an example to watch. MOH's page gives the policy intent and projections, and the real test will be claims data and premium changes in the years after April 2026.

key_points: The new rider design takes effect on April 1, 2026 and applies to riders bought on or after November 27, 2025; insurers decide how to treat riders bought earlier.
New riders must include a co-payment of 5% of the bill, capped at S$6,000 a year, and will not cover the minimum Integrated Shield Plan deductible.
MOH says new riders are on average about 30% cheaper than existing maximum-coverage riders; a 60-year-old on maximum cover could save about S$1,600 a year.
Rider premiums for private hospitals grew an average of 17% a year over the past three years, about double the growth of Integrated Shield Plan premiums.
The minister projects six in ten claimants would pay no cash out-of-pocket after MediSave, and nearly all of the rest would pay S$3,000 or less.
why_it_matters: Riders that cover almost every dollar of a bill can encourage more treatment and push premiums up for everyone. Singapore is trading some cost-sharing for cheaper premiums, a choice that other markets with rising health insurance costs are watching.
